stem: The chapter 'Colonialism and the Countryside' examines how British colonial rule affected rural India, using especially the __________ of the colonial state.
options: Official records and archives (revenue records, surveys, reports)
solution: The chapter examines the impact of British colonial rule on the Indian countryside, and it does so especially by exploring the OFFICIAL RECORDS and archives generated by the colonial state — revenue records, surveys, settlement reports, enquiry commission reports, and the like. A key sub-theme is learning how to read these official sources critically (since they reflect the colonial administration's viewpoint and purposes). So the chapter draws especially on the official records/archives of the colonial state.

stem: The 'Permanent Settlement', a major land-revenue system introduced by the British in 1793 in Bengal (and Bihar), was associated especially with which Governor-General?
solution: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 in Bengal (and Bihar, and later parts of Orissa and Banaras) under the Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. Under it, the revenue to be paid to the state was fixed PERMANENTLY (it was not to be increased in future), and this settlement was made with the ZAMINDARS, who were recognised as the proprietors of the land and were responsible for paying the fixed revenue. So the Permanent Settlement (1793) is associated with Lord Cornwallis.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the revenue was fixed permanently and the settlement was made with the __________, who were made responsible for paying it.
solution: Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the settlement was made with the ZAMINDARS. The zamindars were recognised as the proprietors of the land (with hereditary, saleable rights) and were made responsible for collecting rent from the peasants and paying a PERMANENTLY FIXED amount of revenue to the Company/state. The idea was that a fixed, permanent demand would give zamindars security and an incentive to improve their estates. So the settlement was made with the zamindars.

stem: A key term of the Permanent Settlement was the 'Sunset Law', which stipulated that __________.
options: If a zamindar failed to pay the fixed revenue by the sunset of a specified date, his estate (or part of it) could be auctioned/sold off
Zamindars could only collect rent after sunset
The sun would set the revenue rate
Peasants had to work only until sunset
solution: The 'Sunset Law' was a strict condition of the Permanent Settlement: if a zamindar FAILED to pay the fixed revenue amount in full by the SUNSET of a specified due date, his estate (or a portion of it) could be seized and AUCTIONED/SOLD off by the Company to recover the dues. This rigid rule put enormous pressure on zamindars, and especially in the early decades many defaulted (for various reasons) and lost their estates at auction. So the Sunset Law provided for the auction of a defaulting zamindar's estate. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: In the early years of the Permanent Settlement, many zamindars failed to pay the fixed revenue and lost their lands. This was partly because __________.
options: The revenue demand was fixed very high (and was rigid/inflexible even in bad harvest years), zamindars' own power to collect from ryots was initially curtailed, and prices were often low
There were no peasants to collect rent from
Zamindars refused all payment out of protest
solution: In the early decades of the Permanent Settlement, many zamindars defaulted and lost their estates for several reasons: the initial revenue demand was fixed very HIGH (in the expectation of future agricultural expansion), and it was RIGID/INFLEXIBLE — the same fixed sum had to be paid even in years of poor harvests or low prices; agricultural prices were often depressed in this early period, reducing zamindars' income; and the Company's regulations initially LIMITED the zamindars' own power to coerce rent from the ryots (e.g., restricting their judicial/policing powers). These pressures caused widespread default and the auctioning of estates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The zamindars devised various strategies to avoid losing their estates at auction. One such device was __________.
options: Fictitious/benami sales and manipulation of auctions (e.g., women of the household or servants bidding, or agents buying back the estate)
solution: To survive the harsh terms of the settlement and avoid genuinely losing their estates at auction, zamindars devised various strategies and manipulations. One notable device was resorting to FICTITIOUS/benami sales and manipulating the auctions: for example, the zamindar's own agents, servants, or even the women of his household would put in bids and 'buy' the estate at the auction (so it stayed in the family's control), or agents would refuse to pay so the estate could be bought back cheaply, or dues would be transferred among family members. Through such manoeuvres, many zamindars managed to retain effective control of their estates. So one device was fictitious/benami auction manipulation.

stem: The area around Bengal known for a great uprising of tribal peasants against moneylenders and the colonial order, discussed in the chapter, is associated with the __________.
options: Santhals (the Santhal rebellion of 1855–56) and the region of Rajmahal hills / 'Damin-i-Koh'
solution: The chapter discusses the Santhals — a tribal/adivasi people — and their great uprising, the Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56, against the oppression of moneylenders (dikus), zamindars, and the colonial authorities. The Santhals had been settled in a demarcated tract of the Rajmahal hills area known as the 'Damin-i-Koh' ('skirts of the hills'), where they cleared forest and cultivated, but they came to be exploited by moneylenders and traders and burdened by revenue, leading to their revolt. So the uprising is associated with the Santhals and the Rajmahal hills/Damin-i-Koh.

stem: The Santhals were settled by the colonial authorities in a demarcated forest tract called the 'Damin-i-Koh'. There they were expected to __________.
options: Clear the forest and practise settled cultivation (becoming settled peasants who would pay revenue)
solution: The colonial authorities demarcated a tract of land in the Rajmahal hills region — the 'Damin-i-Koh' — and settled the Santhals there, expecting them to CLEAR the forest and take up SETTLED (plough) CULTIVATION, transforming into settled peasants who would expand the arable and pay land revenue to the state. The Santhals did clear forests and cultivate, but they were soon squeezed by high revenue demands, and above all by exploitative moneylenders and traders (dikus) who trapped them in debt and seized their lands — grievances that led to the 1855–56 rebellion. So they were settled to clear forest and practise settled cultivation.

stem: The moneylenders and traders whom the Santhals blamed for their oppression (and against whom they revolted) were referred to as __________.
solution: The Santhals referred to the moneylenders, traders, and outsiders who exploited them — trapping them in debt at exorbitant interest, cheating them, and seizing their lands and produce — as 'dikus' (meaning 'outsiders'). Resentment against the dikus (along with oppressive zamindars, the police, and the colonial revenue burden) was a central grievance behind the Santhal rebellion of 1855–56. So the exploitative moneylenders/outsiders were the dikus. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: The Santhal rebellion (1855–56) was led by the brothers __________.
options: Sidhu and Kanhu (Sido and Kanhu Murmu)
solution: The Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56 was led by the brothers Sidhu (Sido) and Kanhu (Kanhu) Murmu, along with their brothers Chand and Bhairav. They mobilised thousands of Santhals to rise up against the dikus (moneylenders/traders), the zamindars, and the colonial authorities, aiming to end their oppression and establish their own rule/just order. The rebellion was eventually suppressed with much bloodshed by the British. So the leaders were Sidhu and Kanhu. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Fifth Report, an important colonial document referred to in the chapter, was __________.
options: A report submitted to the British Parliament in 1813 on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India (including revenue and the state of the countryside)
solution: The 'Fifth Report' was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the English East India Company in India, submitted to the BRITISH PARLIAMENT in 1813. It was a voluminous document (running to over a thousand pages) containing information and appendices on the revenue system, the condition of the countryside, the zamindars and ryots, petitions, and reports of collectors and officials. It became an influential source shaping perceptions of Company rule in India — though historians read it critically, aware of its context (it was produced partly in the context of debates in Britain over the Company's monopoly and conduct). So the Fifth Report was a 1813 report to the British Parliament.

stem: Historians caution that the Fifth Report, though valuable, must be read critically because it __________.
options: Was shaped by the political context in Britain (debates over the Company) and tended to exaggerate the decline/mismanagement to serve particular arguments; and it reflected an official viewpoint
Was purely fictional with no basis
solution: Historians caution that the Fifth Report, while a rich source, must be read CRITICALLY. It was produced within a particular POLITICAL context in Britain — there were vigorous debates about the East India Company (including attacks on its monopoly and its conduct in India), and those who compiled and used the Report had their own agendas. As a result, the Report tended to EXAGGERATE the decline of local society and the mismanagement/oppression under the Company (and under the older zamindari order) to serve certain arguments, and it reflected an official, outsider viewpoint. So it must be read with awareness of its context and biases. So option 1 is correct. This is a key methodological point about using colonial records.

stem: In the Bombay Deccan, the British introduced a different revenue system (not the Permanent Settlement) in which the revenue was settled directly with individual cultivators (ryots). This was the __________.
solution: In the Bombay Deccan (and much of southern and western India), the British introduced the RYOTWARI system, in which the revenue settlement was made DIRECTLY with the individual cultivators (the ryots) rather than with zamindars. Each ryot was held responsible for paying revenue on his own holding, the land was surveyed and assessed, and the revenue was periodically revised (not fixed permanently). This system is the backdrop to the chapter's discussion of the Deccan ryots, their indebtedness, and the Deccan Riots. So the Deccan system was the ryotwari system.

stem: Under the ryotwari system in the Deccan, the revenue demand was __________ (unlike the Permanent Settlement).
options: Not fixed permanently — it was periodically revised (re-assessed), and was often set quite high
Paid only in kind, never in cash
solution: Unlike the Permanent Settlement (where the demand was fixed forever), the ryotwari system involved a revenue demand that was NOT permanent: it was periodically REVISED/re-assessed (e.g., every thirty years in some settlements), and it was often set quite HIGH. The high and revisable demand, collected rigidly even in bad years and payable in cash, placed heavy pressure on the Deccan ryots, pushing many into debt with moneylenders — a background cause of the Deccan Riots. So the ryotwari demand was periodically revised and often high. This contrast with the Permanent Settlement is important.

stem: The great agrarian uprising of 1875 in the Bombay Deccan, in which peasants (ryots) attacked moneylenders and destroyed their debt-bonds, is known as the __________.
solution: The Deccan Riots of 1875 were a major agrarian uprising in the Bombay Deccan (beginning in Pune/Poona district, e.g., at Supa, and spreading), in which the ryots (peasants) rose up against the moneylenders (sahukars), attacking them, and seizing and DESTROYING the bonds, deeds, and account-books that recorded their debts (and sometimes burning down houses and shops). The immediate targets were the moneylenders whom the peasants blamed for their oppression and dispossession. So the 1875 uprising is the Deccan Riots. A Deccan Riots Commission was appointed to enquire into its causes.

stem: A major underlying cause of the Deccan Riots was the peasants' mounting __________ to moneylenders.
options: Indebtedness (debt) — ryots had fallen deeply into debt, losing land and dignity to the sahukars
solution: A major underlying cause of the Deccan Riots was the mounting INDEBTEDNESS of the ryots to the moneylenders (sahukars). Squeezed by the high, rigid, cash revenue demand of the ryotwari system, and needing loans (especially after bad harvests and during a slump), the peasants borrowed from moneylenders, who charged high interest, manipulated accounts and bonds, and increasingly seized the peasants' land, produce, and property when debts could not be repaid. The peasants' sense of being cheated and dispossessed, and their resentment at losing land and dignity, boiled over into the attacks on moneylenders. So the underlying cause was peasant indebtedness to moneylenders.

stem: The peasants' anger against the moneylenders in the Deccan intensified after the __________, which had first raised and then collapsed cotton prices/incomes.
options: End of the American Civil War (the cotton boom collapsed around 1865, hurting Deccan cotton growers)
solution: The peasants' distress and anger in the Deccan were intensified by the cotton cycle linked to the American Civil War (1861–65). During the war, cotton exports from the American South were disrupted, so Britain turned to Indian (Deccan) cotton — causing a BOOM: cotton prices and demand soared, and Deccan cotton growers (and moneylenders) expanded credit and cultivation. But when the American Civil War ENDED (around 1865), American cotton returned to the market, the boom COLLAPSED, prices and exports crashed, and Deccan cotton growers' incomes fell sharply — leaving them unable to repay the debts contracted during the boom. This bust deepened indebtedness and grievance, feeding into the 1875 riots. So the trigger was the end of the American Civil War and the cotton price collapse.

stem: After the Deccan Riots, the government appointed a commission to investigate. This shows that the colonial state responded to unrest by __________.
options: Setting up enquiry commissions (like the Deccan Riots Commission) whose reports became sources historians use — while reflecting official concerns and perspectives
solution: In response to the Deccan Riots, the colonial government appointed the Deccan Riots Commission to investigate the causes of the unrest. The Commission gathered evidence — statements from ryots, moneylenders, and officials, and reports and statistics — and produced a report. Such enquiry-commission reports became valuable SOURCES that historians use to reconstruct rural conditions and grievances. However, historians read them critically, because they reflect the OFFICIAL concerns and perspective of the colonial state (for instance, the Commission was keen to establish whether the government's own revenue demand was to blame, and tended to shift blame onto the moneylenders). So the state responded via enquiry commissions whose reports are useful but partial sources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Deccan Riots Commission's report tended to __________, reflecting the colonial government's reluctance to blame its own policies.
options: Place the blame primarily on the moneylenders, while downplaying the role of the government's high revenue demand
solution: The Deccan Riots Commission's report tended to place the blame for the peasants' distress primarily on the MONEYLENDERS (the sahukars) and their exploitative practices, while DOWNPLAYING or denying the role of the GOVERNMENT's own high revenue demand in impoverishing the ryots. This reflected the colonial government's reluctance to hold its own revenue policy responsible for the unrest. Historians therefore read the report critically, recognising this bias, and use it (along with other evidence) to reconstruct the real causes — which included both the moneylenders' exploitation and the heavy state demand. So the report shifted blame onto the moneylenders and away from government policy. This is a key point about reading official records critically.

stem: Which broad point about COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS does the chapter emphasise?
options: They are neutral, complete, and perfectly objective

They are valuable but must be read critically — they were produced by the colonial administration for its own purposes, reflect official perspectives and biases, and often obscure the viewpoints of peasants and other ordinary people
They contain no useful information at all
They were written by the peasants themselves
solution: A central methodological point of the chapter is that COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS (revenue records, surveys, reports like the Fifth Report and the Deccan Riots Commission report) are extremely VALUABLE sources — but they must be read CRITICALLY. They were produced by the colonial administration for its OWN purposes (chiefly revenue collection and control), and they inevitably reflect the OFFICIAL perspective, assumptions, and biases of the colonial state (and of those who compiled them). Crucially, they often OBSCURE or distort the viewpoints, experiences, and voices of the peasants and other ordinary rural people. So historians must interrogate these records carefully — reading 'against the grain', corroborating with other evidence, and being alert to what is left out. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The Permanent Settlement, by making the revenue demand fixed and permanent, was expected by the British to __________ — though the results were mixed.
options: Give zamindars a secure incentive to invest in and improve agriculture (and provide the state with a stable, assured income)
solution: The British EXPECTED the Permanent Settlement to bring several benefits: by fixing the revenue demand PERMANENTLY, it would give the zamindars security and a strong INCENTIVE to invest in and IMPROVE their estates and agriculture (since any increase in produce/income above the fixed demand would be theirs to keep), thereby raising agricultural productivity; and it would give the STATE a STABLE, ASSURED income (a fixed sum) and create a loyal class of landed proprietors. In practice, however, the RESULTS were MIXED and often disappointing: many zamindars initially defaulted and lost their estates, the expected agricultural improvement was often not realised, the rigidity hurt in bad years, and the burden was passed onto the ryots. So the intention was to give zamindars an incentive to improve and give the state stable income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the ultimate burden of the revenue demand often fell on the __________, who were squeezed by the zamindars.
options: Ryots (peasants/cultivators), through high rents and various cesses
solution: Although the Permanent Settlement was made with the zamindars, the ultimate BURDEN of the revenue demand often fell on the RYOTS (the actual peasant cultivators). To meet the fixed revenue payable to the state (and to profit), zamindars extracted high RENTS and various additional cesses/levies from the peasants, and could evict or coerce them. The peasants thus bore the weight of the system, often with little security of tenure and subject to exactions. So the burden fell on the ryots. This shows how the settlement, made with zamindars, ultimately pressed down on the cultivators.

stem: The term 'jotedars', mentioned in the context of Bengal's countryside, refers to __________.
options: Rich peasants/landholders who controlled large areas, lent money, and grew powerful in the villages (sometimes at the expense of the zamindars)
solution: In the Bengal countryside, the jotedars were a class of RICH PEASANTS/landholders who, over time, acquired control of large areas of land, dominated local trade and moneylending, and grew POWERFUL in the villages. As many zamindars (especially absentee ones) weakened under the pressures of the Permanent Settlement, the jotedars — being resident and locally rooted — often gained at the zamindars' expense, controlling the actual cultivators (many of whom were their sharecroppers/adhiyars), resisting the zamindars' demands, and even acquiring zamindari lands at auctions. They represent an important rural power group that rose under colonial conditions. So jotedars were rich, powerful village landholders. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: The jotedars were often more powerful than the zamindars in the actual villages because they __________.
options: Were resident in the countryside (not absentee), directly controlled the cultivators and local trade/credit, and could resist the zamindars' demands
Owned the British East India Company
solution: The jotedars were often more powerful than the zamindars WITHIN the villages because: they were RESIDENT in the countryside (whereas many zamindars were absentee, living in towns), giving them direct, on-the-ground control; they directly controlled a large body of poorer cultivators and SHARECROPPERS (adhiyars/bargadars, who cultivated the jotedars' land and gave a share of the produce); they dominated local TRADE and MONEYLENDING; and they were well-placed to RESIST the zamindars' demands for revenue/rent and to frustrate their authority (even buying up zamindari estates when these were auctioned). This local rootedness and control made them formidable. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rich peasants and moneylenders who exploited the ryots, and the strategies of zamindars and jotedars, together show that colonialism reshaped rural society by __________.
options: Creating new pressures and opportunities that produced winners and losers — strengthening some groups (like certain moneylenders and rich peasants/jotedars) while impoverishing and dispossessing many ordinary peasants and tribal cultivators
solution: The various developments the chapter traces — the fortunes of zamindars under the Permanent Settlement, the rise of jotedars, the indebtedness and dispossession of Deccan ryots to moneylenders, and the exploitation and revolt of the Santhals — together show that COLONIALISM RESHAPED rural society by creating new economic and administrative pressures AND opportunities that produced WINNERS and LOSERS. Some groups (certain moneylenders, rich peasants/jotedars, and surviving/adaptive zamindars) gained power and wealth, while many ordinary peasants and tribal cultivators were impoverished, indebted, and dispossessed — sometimes to the point of rebellion. Rural society was thus transformed, differentiated, and often destabilised (not made equal or left unchanged). So option 2 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Many Bengal zamindars lost their estates in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement. Reason (R): The revenue demand was fixed very high and had to be paid rigidly by a fixed date (the Sunset Law), regardless of harvests or prices. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that many Bengal zamindars lost their estates (through auction) in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement. And the reason is (R) that the revenue demand was fixed very HIGH and had to be paid RIGIDLY and in full by a fixed due date under the Sunset Law — regardless of whether the harvest was good or bad, or prices high or low — so that any failure to pay on time led to the estate being auctioned. This harsh, inflexible fiscal regime (together with low prices and curbs on zamindars' collecting power) directly caused the widespread defaults and loss of estates (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Deccan ryots attacked moneylenders and burnt their bonds and deeds in 1875. Reason (R): The peasants saw the moneylenders' account-books and debt-bonds as instruments of their oppression and dispossession. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that during the Deccan Riots of 1875 the ryots attacked the moneylenders and specifically SEIZED and BURNT/destroyed their bonds, deeds, and account-books. And the reason is (R) that the peasants saw these documents — the debt-bonds and manipulated account-books through which the moneylenders enforced debts, extracted exorbitant interest, and seized land — as the very INSTRUMENTS of their oppression and dispossession. By destroying these records, the ryots aimed to wipe out the legal/documentary basis of their debts and the moneylenders' hold over them. So the peasants' view of the bonds as tools of oppression directly explains why they targeted and burnt them (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in which year?
solution: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal (and Bihar) in 1793 under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. It permanently fixed the land-revenue demand and settled it with the zamindars. (1757 was the Battle of Plassey; 1857 the Revolt; 1905 the first Partition of Bengal.) So the Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793.

stem: The poorer cultivators in Bengal who cultivated the jotedars' land as sharecroppers, giving a share of the produce, were called __________.
solution: In the Bengal countryside, the poorer cultivators who worked the land of the rich jotedars as sharecroppers — cultivating the land and handing over a share (often half) of the produce to the jotedar — were called adhiyars or bargadars. They were dependent on the jotedars for land, ploughs, and credit, and formed the lower rung of the rural hierarchy the jotedars dominated. So the sharecroppers were the adhiyars/bargadars.

stem: The village where the Deccan Riots of 1875 began (the initial outbreak against a moneylender) was __________, in Poona (Pune) district.
solution: The Deccan Riots of 1875 first broke out at Supa, a market village (in Poona/Pune district of the Bombay Deccan), where ryots rose against a local moneylender, attacking him and seizing and destroying the debt-bonds and account-books. From Supa the unrest spread to other villages and districts (like Ahmednagar). So the riots began at Supa.

stem: During the cotton boom of the 1860s, credit flowed freely to Deccan cotton growers. When the boom ended, the moneylenders __________.
options: Refused further loans and pressed hard for repayment of existing debts, tightening the squeeze on the ryots
solution: During the cotton boom of the 1860s (fuelled by the American Civil War), moneylenders had extended credit freely to Deccan cotton growers, who expanded cultivation and borrowing. When the boom COLLAPSED (after the American Civil War ended and prices crashed around 1865), the moneylenders REFUSED to extend further loans and instead pressed hard for the REPAYMENT of the existing debts. This sudden tightening — demanding repayment when incomes had collapsed — deepened the ryots' distress, dispossession, and resentment, feeding into the 1875 riots. So the moneylenders refused new loans and demanded repayment.

stem: The peasants of the Deccan felt a deep sense of injustice partly because the moneylenders were seen as violating the customary norms of __________.
options: Fair dealing/honest lending (e.g., charging exorbitant interest, manipulating accounts, and refusing to give receipts)
solution: The Deccan peasants' sense of moral outrage stemmed partly from their feeling that the moneylenders had VIOLATED the customary norms of FAIR DEALING and honest lending. The peasants complained that moneylenders charged exorbitant/usurious interest, manipulated and falsified account-books and bonds (e.g., inflating the amounts owed), refused to give receipts for payments made, and used legal and fraudulent means to seize the peasants' land and property. This breach of customary fairness — the sense of being cheated and dishonoured, not just indebted — helped turn economic distress into moral anger and violent protest. So the moneylenders were seen as violating norms of fair/honest dealing.

stem: The new legal system introduced under colonial rule affected peasant–moneylender relations because __________.
options: Written deeds/bonds and the courts gave moneylenders a powerful legal means to enforce debts and seize land (often against illiterate peasants who signed documents they could not read)
There were no courts at all
Peasants could never be taken to court
solution: The colonial legal system reshaped peasant–moneylender relations to the peasants' disadvantage. The emphasis on WRITTEN documents — deeds, bonds, and account-books — and the availability of COURTS gave moneylenders a powerful LEGAL means to enforce debts and to seize the peasants' land and property when debts went unpaid. Illiterate peasants often signed bonds and documents they could not read or fully understand (and whose terms the moneylenders could manipulate), and the courts tended to uphold these written instruments. Thus the legal system, and the sanctity it gave to written contracts, strengthened the moneylenders' hold over the peasants. So the new legal system empowered moneylenders to enforce debts legally. This is an important point.

stem: The colonial officials who were responsible for collecting revenue and administering districts, and who produced many of the reports and records, were the __________.
solution: Under colonial rule, the officials chiefly responsible for collecting land revenue and administering the districts were the Collectors (the district Collectors) and their subordinate revenue officials/surveyors. The office of the Collector became central to the colonial rural administration, and it was these officials who conducted surveys, kept revenue records, and wrote the reports and correspondence that make up much of the colonial archive on the countryside. So the key revenue/administrative officials were the Collectors. Their records are a major (but partial and official) source.

stem: The chapter emphasises that to write the history of the countryside, historians must go 'against the grain' of official records. This means they should __________.
options: Read the records critically — questioning the assumptions and silences of the official viewpoint, and trying to recover the perspectives (of peasants, tribals) that the records marginalise or distort
Accept every official statement as literal truth
Only read the grain harvest reports
solution: Reading official records 'against the grain' means reading them CRITICALLY rather than at face value: questioning the ASSUMPTIONS, purposes, and biases built into the official/colonial viewpoint; attending to what the records leave out or distort (their SILENCES); and trying to recover, as far as possible, the perspectives and experiences of the peasants, tribals, and other ordinary people whom the official records tend to marginalise, misrepresent, or ignore. Since the colonial archive was produced by the administration for its own ends, historians must interrogate it and read between the lines (and use other evidence) to reconstruct rural realities. So going 'against the grain' means reading the records critically to recover marginalised perspectives. This is a central methodological theme.

stem: The colonial state's drive to survey, map, and record the land in minute detail reflected its interest in __________.
options: Controlling and taxing the countryside effectively (knowledge as a tool of colonial power and revenue extraction)
solution: The colonial state's enormous effort to survey, measure, map, classify, and record the land and its produce in minute detail reflected its interest in CONTROLLING and TAXING the countryside effectively. Detailed knowledge of landholdings, cultivators, crops, and yields enabled the state to assess and maximise land revenue and to administer and control rural society — an example of how KNOWLEDGE served as a tool of colonial POWER and revenue extraction. The vast archive this generated is what historians now use (critically). So the surveys served colonial control and revenue extraction. This links the archive to the purposes of colonial rule.

stem: Which statement about the impact of the Permanent Settlement on Bengal agriculture over the longer term is generally accepted?
options: It rapidly modernised agriculture and enriched the peasants
It largely failed to produce the expected agricultural improvement/investment; zamindars often became rentiers extracting rent rather than improving landlords, and the burden pressed on the ryots
solution: Over the longer term, the Permanent Settlement is generally seen as having LARGELY FAILED to deliver the agricultural improvement and investment the British had hoped for. Rather than becoming enterprising 'improving landlords', many zamindars functioned as RENTIERS — content to extract rent from the peasants without investing in improving the land or agriculture. Meanwhile, the fixed revenue benefited the state's stability but the actual burden was passed down onto the RYOTS (through high rents and cesses), who gained little security or prosperity. So the settlement failed to modernise agriculture; zamindars became rent-extractors and the ryots bore the burden. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The Santhals, before being settled in the Damin-i-Koh, were encouraged to move there because the colonial authorities wanted to __________.
options: Extend settled cultivation and revenue into the hill/forest tracts (the Paharias, the earlier hill people, had resisted, so the Santhals were brought in as pioneer cultivators)
solution: The colonial authorities wanted to EXTEND settled plough cultivation (and hence revenue) into the hill and forest tracts of the Rajmahal region. The earlier hill people, the PAHARIAS, practised shifting cultivation and hunting-gathering and RESISTED settled agriculture and outside control. So the British encouraged the SANTHALS to move in and settle the demarcated Damin-i-Koh tract as PIONEER cultivators who would clear the forest and expand settled farming. The Santhals thus came to occupy the foothills, displacing/marginalising the Paharias, but were themselves soon exploited by moneylenders and the revenue burden — leading to their revolt. So the Santhals were brought in to extend settled cultivation where the Paharias had resisted. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The earlier hill people of the Rajmahal region, who practised shifting cultivation and hunting and resisted colonial encroachment, were the __________.
solution: The Paharias were the hill people of the Rajmahal region who lived in and around the forests, practising shifting (jhum) cultivation, hunting, and gathering forest produce, and who fiercely resisted the encroachment of outsiders and settled agriculture on their lands. Their conflict with the expanding settled/colonial order — and their marginalisation as the Santhals were settled in the foothills (Damin-i-Koh) — forms part of the background to the region's history in the chapter. So the earlier hill people were the Paharias.

stem: The Santhal rebellion of 1855–56 ultimately resulted in __________.
options: The rebellion being crushed by the British with great force, but afterwards the creation of a separate 'Santhal Pargana' with some special provisions
The abolition of the British Empire
solution: The Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56 was ultimately CRUSHED by the British with great military force and much bloodshed (thousands of Santhals were killed). However, in its aftermath, the colonial authorities recognised the need to address Santhal grievances and administer the area differently: they created a separate administrative district, the Santhal Pargana(s), carved out with some special provisions and rules intended to protect the Santhals (e.g., restrictions on the transfer of Santhal land to outsiders/moneylenders). So the rebellion was crushed but led to the creation of the Santhal Pargana. This is a prelims-relevant outcome.

stem: The account-books and bonds of moneylenders, though produced to record debts, are useful to historians because they __________.
options: Provide detailed evidence about credit, prices, transactions, and rural economic relations (when read critically alongside other sources)
Are always completely honest and unbiased
Tell us nothing about the economy
solution: The moneylenders' account-books, bonds, and deeds — though created to record and enforce debts (and often manipulated) — are useful HISTORICAL sources because they provide detailed evidence about credit and lending, interest rates, prices, transactions, landholdings, and the economic relations between peasants and moneylenders in the countryside. Read CRITICALLY and alongside other sources (like official reports and the peasants' own testimony to enquiry commissions), they help historians reconstruct the workings of the rural credit economy and the pressures on the peasantry. So they provide detailed evidence about credit and rural economic relations, used critically. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One reason the ryots of the Deccan fell into debt was the requirement to pay revenue in __________, even in years of poor harvest.
solution: A key reason Deccan ryots fell into debt was that the revenue had to be paid in CASH (money), by fixed dates, regardless of whether the harvest was good or bad. To obtain the cash — especially in years of poor harvest, low prices, or after the collapse of the cotton boom — the peasants were forced to BORROW from moneylenders (often at high interest), sinking them into debt. The rigid cash demand, collected inflexibly, was thus a structural driver of indebtedness. So the ryots had to pay revenue in cash even in bad years, driving them to borrow. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which pair correctly matches the region with its main British revenue system?
options: Bengal — Permanent Settlement (zamindari); Bombay Deccan/Madras — Ryotwari
solution: The correct matching is: BENGAL (and Bihar) — the Permanent Settlement (a zamindari system, revenue settled with zamindars, demand fixed permanently, 1793, Cornwallis); and the BOMBAY DECCAN and MADRAS regions — the Ryotwari system (revenue settled directly with individual ryots/cultivators, demand periodically revised). (A third system, the Mahalwari, was used in parts of North India/North-Western Provinces, settling revenue with villages/mahals.) So option 1 correctly pairs Bengal with the Permanent Settlement and the Deccan with the Ryotwari system. This is prelims-relevant.

stem: The chapter shows that peasant protests (like the Santhal rebellion and the Deccan Riots) were __________.
options: Responses to real grievances and exploitation (revenue burdens, indebtedness, dispossession, and the breach of customary rights), often targeting the specific agents of their oppression
Purely religious with no economic basis
solution: The chapter demonstrates that peasant and tribal protests such as the Santhal rebellion (1855–56) and the Deccan Riots (1875) were NOT mindless or causeless outbursts. They were RESPONSES to real, concrete grievances and exploitation — heavy and rigid revenue burdens, crushing indebtedness, dispossession and loss of land, and the violation of customary rights and norms of fairness — under the pressures created by colonial rule. And they typically TARGETED the specific agents of that oppression (the moneylenders/dikus and sahukars, oppressive zamindars, and sometimes officials), often in symbolically meaningful ways (like destroying debt-bonds). So the protests were rational responses to genuine grievances, directed at the agents of oppression. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The historian's task in this chapter is often to reconstruct the peasant's world 'from documents that were not written by peasants'. This highlights the problem of __________.
options: The near-absence of direct peasant voices/records — most sources are official or elite, so the peasants' own perspective must be inferred and carefully reconstructed
The peasants writing all the records themselves
There being no documents at all
solution: A key challenge the chapter highlights is that the surviving sources for rural history were, for the most part, NOT written by the peasants themselves — they are official records (surveys, reports, revenue records), or the documents of moneylenders and elites. The peasants, being largely illiterate and voiceless in the archive, left few direct records of their own. So historians face the problem of the near-ABSENCE of direct peasant voices, and must reconstruct the peasants' world and perspective INDIRECTLY and carefully — reading the elite/official sources critically and 'against the grain', and piecing together fragments (like peasant testimony recorded in enquiry commissions) to recover their experience. So it highlights the problem of the absence of direct peasant voices. This is a central methodological insight.

stem: Assertion (A): The Santhals rose in rebellion in 1855–56. Reason (R): They were being exploited by moneylenders (dikus), burdened by revenue, and losing their lands, and they sought to end this oppression and establish their own rule. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Santhals rose in rebellion (the hool) in 1855–56. And the reason is (R) that they were being exploited by the moneylenders and traders (dikus) — who trapped them in debt and seized their lands — burdened by the colonial revenue demand, and dispossessed, and that they rose up to END this oppression and establish their own just rule/order. These grievances and aims were precisely what drove the rebellion (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Colonial official records are indispensable for writing the history of the countryside. Reason (R): Because such records reflect the perspectives and purposes of the colonial state, they must nonetheless be read critically and supplemented with other evidence. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not a contradiction of A (both hold together)
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
solution: Both statements are true and hold together (they are not contradictory). It is true (A) that colonial official records — surveys, revenue records, reports like the Fifth Report and the Deccan Riots Commission report — are INDISPENSABLE for writing the history of the colonial countryside, since they contain a vast amount of otherwise unavailable information. And it is also true (R) that BECAUSE these records reflect the perspectives, assumptions, and purposes of the colonial state, they must be read CRITICALLY and supplemented/corroborated with other evidence to arrive at a balanced understanding. Both propositions are valid simultaneously: the records are essential AND must be used critically. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rise of the jotedars and the survival strategies of the zamindars in Bengal together show that __________.
options: The colonial revenue system had no local impact
Local groups actively responded to, exploited, and reshaped the opportunities and pressures created by colonial policy (rural power relations were dynamic, not simply dictated from above)
The British controlled every detail of village life directly
solution: The rise of the jotedars (rich peasants who gained power locally) and the various survival strategies of the zamindars (like manipulating auctions through fictitious sales) together show that LOCAL GROUPS actively RESPONDED to, EXPLOITED, and RESHAPED the opportunities and pressures created by colonial policy. Rural power relations were DYNAMIC and contested — not simply imposed from above by the colonial state. Colonial policy set new conditions, but Indians (zamindars, jotedars, moneylenders, peasants) manoeuvred within them, and the actual outcomes on the ground emerged from these local struggles and adaptations. So option 2 is correct — it underscores the agency of local groups and the dynamism of rural society under colonialism.

stem: Taken together, the Bengal and Deccan case studies in the chapter illustrate the broader point that colonial land-revenue policies __________.
options: Varied by region (Permanent Settlement vs Ryotwari) but commonly increased the pressure on the actual cultivators, fostered indebtedness and social differentiation, and generated distress and resistance in the countryside
Had identical effects everywhere with no regional variation
Left the peasants wealthier and more secure
solution: Taken together, the Bengal (Permanent Settlement) and Deccan (Ryotwari) case studies illustrate a broader point: colonial land-revenue policies VARIED by region in their form (settling revenue with zamindars in Bengal, with individual ryots in the Deccan), but they commonly INCREASED the pressure on the actual CULTIVATORS, fostered widespread INDEBTEDNESS and social DIFFERENTIATION (creating rural winners like jotedars and moneylenders, and losers among the ordinary peasantry and tribals), and generated agrarian DISTRESS and RESISTANCE (from the Santhal rebellion to the Deccan Riots). So despite regional differences, the systems tended to burden cultivators and destabilise the countryside. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal (and Bihar) in the year:
solution: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793.

stem: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was associated especially with which Governor-General?
solution: The Permanent Settlement is associated with Lord Cornwallis.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the revenue was fixed permanently and settled with the __________, who were responsible for paying it.
solution: The Permanent Settlement was made with the zamindars, who were fixed as revenue-payers to the state.

stem: The 'Sunset Law' of the Permanent Settlement stipulated that:
options: if the fixed revenue was not paid by sunset of a specified date, the zamindar's estate could be auctioned
solution: Under the Sunset Law, if the fixed revenue was not paid by sunset on the specified date, the estate could be auctioned off.

stem: Many Bengal zamindars lost their estates in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement partly because:
options: the revenue demand was fixed very high and had to be paid rigidly regardless of harvests or prices
solution: The high fixed revenue and the rigid Sunset Law meant many zamindars failed to pay (especially in bad years) and lost their estates.

stem: To avoid losing their estates at auction, zamindars devised strategies such as:
options: fictitious sales, transferring land to female relatives, or using agents (benamdars) to buy back their own estates
solution: Zamindars used devices like fictitious sales, transfers to relatives, and agents (benamdars) to buy back their own auctioned estates.

stem: The 'jotedars' in Bengal's countryside were:
options: rich peasants who had acquired large landholdings and controlled local trade and moneylending
solution: The jotedars were rich peasants who had built up large landholdings and controlled local trade and moneylending in the villages.

stem: The jotedars were often more powerful than the zamindars in the villages because they:
options: were based in the villages, controlled the poorer cultivators, and could resist the zamindar's demands
solution: Being resident in the villages and controlling the poorer cultivators and local credit, the jotedars could effectively resist the zamindars.

stem: The poorer cultivators who worked the jotedars' land as sharecroppers, giving a share of the produce, were called:
solution: The sharecroppers who cultivated the jotedars' land for a share of the produce were called adhiyars or bargadars.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the ultimate burden of the revenue demand often fell on the:
options: ryots (peasants), who were squeezed by the zamindars
solution: The revenue burden was largely passed on to the ryots (peasants), who were squeezed by the zamindars to meet the fixed demand.

stem: The Fifth Report, an important colonial document, was:
options: a report submitted to the British Parliament (1813) on the administration and revenue of the East India Company in India
solution: The Fifth Report (1813) was submitted to the British Parliament on the administration and revenue affairs of the East India Company in India.

stem: Historians caution that the Fifth Report must be read critically because it:
options: was shaped by the concerns and biases of those who compiled it (often to criticise Company rule) and may exaggerate
solution: The Fifth Report reflected the concerns and biases of its compilers (partly critics of Company rule) and could exaggerate, so it must be read critically.

stem: The Santhals were settled by the colonial authorities in a demarcated forest tract called the:
solution: The Santhals were settled in the 'Damin-i-Koh', a demarcated forest tract, where they were expected to clear forest and farm.

stem: In the Damin-i-Koh, the Santhals were expected to:
options: clear the forest and settle down to plough agriculture (become settled peasants)
solution: The Santhals were expected to clear the forest and settle down as plough-cultivators, producing revenue.

stem: The moneylenders and traders whom the Santhals blamed for their oppression were called:
solution: The Santhals called the exploiting moneylenders and traders 'dikus' (outsiders).

stem: The Santhal rebellion (1855–56) was led by the brothers:
solution: The Santhal rebellion of 1855–56 was led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu (Murmu).

stem: The earlier hill people of the Rajmahal region, who practised shifting cultivation and hunting and resisted colonial encroachment, were the:
solution: The Paharias were the earlier hill people of the Rajmahal region who practised shifting cultivation and hunting and resisted the colonial advance.

stem: The Santhal rebellion of 1855–56 ultimately resulted in:
options: its suppression by the colonial state, but also the creation of a separate Santhal Pargana
solution: The rebellion was suppressed, but it led the government to create a separate Santhal Pargana with some protective measures.

stem: In the Bombay Deccan, the British introduced a revenue system settled directly with individual cultivators (ryots), called the:
solution: In the Bombay Deccan, the British introduced the Ryotwari system, settling revenue directly with individual ryots (cultivators).

stem: Under the ryotwari system, the revenue demand was __________, unlike the Permanent Settlement.
solution: Under ryotwari, the revenue demand was periodically revised (resettled), unlike the permanently fixed Bengal settlement.

stem: The ryots of the Deccan often fell into debt because they had to pay revenue in __________, even in years of poor harvest.
solution: The requirement to pay revenue in cash, even in poor harvest years, drove the ryots to borrow from moneylenders, deepening their debt.

stem: The great agrarian uprising of 1875 in the Bombay Deccan, in which ryots attacked moneylenders and destroyed debt-bonds, is known as the:
solution: The 1875 uprising in the Deccan is known as the Deccan Riots.

stem: The village where the Deccan Riots of 1875 began, in Poona (Pune) district, was:
solution: The Deccan Riots began at Supa, in Poona (Pune) district.

stem: The peasants' anger in the Deccan intensified after the __________, which first raised and then collapsed cotton incomes.
options: American Civil War (cotton boom of the 1860s)
solution: The American Civil War (1861–65) caused a cotton boom, then its end collapsed cotton prices/incomes, intensifying peasant distress and anger.

stem: During the cotton boom of the 1860s, when the boom ended, the moneylenders:
options: tightened credit and pressed the ryots hard for repayment
solution: When the boom ended, moneylenders tightened credit and pressed the indebted ryots hard, fuelling resentment.

stem: The Deccan ryots targeted the moneylenders' __________, seeing them as instruments of oppression.
solution: The ryots attacked and burnt the moneylenders' account-books, bonds and deeds, seeing them as instruments of their dispossession.

stem: The peasants felt a deep sense of injustice because the moneylenders were seen as violating the customary norms of:
options: fair dealing (e.g., charging exorbitant interest and manipulating accounts)
solution: The moneylenders were seen as violating customary norms of fair dealing — charging exorbitant interest, manipulating accounts and seizing land.

stem: The new colonial legal system affected peasant-moneylender relations because:
options: it enforced written bonds/contracts strictly, favouring the moneylenders and enabling them to seize peasants' land legally
solution: The new legal system strictly enforced written contracts/bonds, which favoured moneylenders and let them legally seize the land of indebted peasants.

stem: After the Deccan Riots, the government appointed the Deccan Riots Commission, showing that the colonial state:
options: responded to unrest by investigating (partly to protect its interests and revenue)
solution: The appointment of the Deccan Riots Commission shows the state responded to unrest by investigating, partly out of concern for order and its revenue.

stem: The Deccan Riots Commission's report tended to:
options: downplay the role of colonial revenue policy and put blame elsewhere (e.g., on moneylenders)
solution: The Commission tended to downplay the role of colonial revenue policy, reflecting the government's reluctance to blame its own policies.

stem: The colonial officials responsible for collecting revenue and administering districts, who produced many records, were the:
solution: The Collectors and other district revenue officials administered districts and produced many of the records historians use.

stem: To write the history of the countryside, historians must read official records 'against the grain', meaning they should:
options: read them critically, questioning their assumptions and biases and looking for what they leave out or distort
solution: Reading 'against the grain' means reading official records critically — questioning their assumptions and biases and recovering the perspectives they omit or distort.

stem: The moneylenders' account-books and bonds, though produced to record debts, are useful to historians because they:
options: shed light on peasant-moneylender relations, rural credit and the process of dispossession
solution: Such records illuminate peasant-moneylender relations, the workings of rural credit, and how peasants were dispossessed.

stem: The colonial state's drive to survey, map and record the land in detail reflected its interest in:
options: maximising and securing land revenue (and control over resources)
solution: The detailed surveys and records served the state's interest in maximising and securing land revenue and control over rural resources.

stem: Which statement about the long-term impact of the Permanent Settlement on Bengal agriculture is generally accepted?
options: it did not lead to the expected agricultural investment/improvement, and burdened the peasants
solution: The Permanent Settlement generally failed to bring the expected agricultural investment and improvement, while burdening the peasants — its results were disappointing.

stem: The rise of the jotedars and the survival strategies of the zamindars together show that:
options: colonial land policy reshaped rural power, creating new dominant groups and struggles over land
solution: They show that colonial land-revenue policy reshaped rural power relations, creating new dominant groups (jotedars) and struggles over land and revenue.

stem: Colonialism reshaped rural society by __________, as shown by the strategies of zamindars, jotedars and moneylenders.
options: creating new pressures, groups and conflicts over land, revenue and debt
solution: Colonial policies created new economic pressures, new dominant groups and new conflicts over land, revenue and debt in the countryside.

stem: The peasant protests (the Santhal rebellion and the Deccan Riots) were:
options: expressions of genuine grievances against exploitation and colonial policies, revealing the tensions in the countryside
solution: The protests expressed genuine grievances against exploitation (by moneylenders) and colonial policies, revealing the deep tensions in the colonial countryside.

stem: The historian's task of reconstructing the peasant's world 'from documents not written by peasants' highlights the problem of:
options: the scarcity of the peasants' own voice, so their history must be recovered from records written by others (officials, moneylenders)
solution: It highlights that peasants left few records of their own, so their history must be reconstructed critically from documents written by others.

stem: Assertion (A): Many Bengal zamindars lost their estates in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement. Reason (R): The revenue demand was fixed very high and had to be paid rigidly by a fixed date (the Sunset Law), regardless of harvests. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: the high fixed demand and the rigid Sunset Law caused many zamindars to default and lose their estates.

stem: Assertion (A): The Deccan ryots attacked moneylenders and burnt their bonds in 1875. Reason (R): The peasants saw the moneylenders' account-books and debt-bonds as instruments of their oppression and dispossession. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: seeing the bonds as tools of their dispossession, the ryots attacked moneylenders and burnt their deeds.

stem: Assertion (A): The Santhals rose in rebellion in 1855–56. Reason (R): They were exploited by moneylenders (dikus), burdened by revenue and losing their lands, and sought to end this oppression. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: exploitation by dikus, revenue burdens and land loss drove the Santhals to rebel in 1855–56.

stem: Assertion (A): Colonial official records are indispensable for writing the history of the countryside. Reason (R): Because such records reflect the perspectives and purposes of the colonial state, they must be read critically and supplemented with other evidence. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: indispensable but biased, colonial records must be read critically and supplemented with other evidence.

stem: Taken together, the Bengal and Deccan case studies illustrate that colonial land-revenue policies:
options: profoundly disrupted rural society — creating debt, dispossession, new power groups and peasant unrest
solution: The two case studies show that colonial revenue policies profoundly disrupted rural society, causing debt, dispossession, new power groups and peasant unrest.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Colonialism and the Countryside'?
options: British colonial land-revenue policies (like the Permanent Settlement and Ryotwari) reshaped and often disrupted rural India — causing debt, dispossession and revolts — and their history must be recovered by reading colonial records critically
solution: The chapter concludes that British colonial land-revenue policies reshaped and often disrupted rural India — causing debt, dispossession and revolts — and that their history must be reconstructed by reading colonial records critically alongside other evidence.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Colonialism and the Countryside' is that:
options: British rule had no effect on rural India

British colonial rule profoundly transformed the Indian countryside — through revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement in Bengal (fixed demand, settlement with zamindars, the Sunset Law, defaults, and the rise of jotedars) and the ryotwari system in the Deccan (high, revisable demand, ryot indebtedness to moneylenders, and the Deccan Riots of 1875), and through the settlement and exploitation of tribal peoples like the Santhals (leading to their 1855–56 rebellion) — producing winners and losers, deepening indebtedness and dispossession, and provoking resistance; and this history is reconstructed largely from colonial official records (like the Fifth Report and enquiry-commission reports), which are valuable but must be read critically for their official biases
The countryside was prosperous and contented under colonial rule
Only the Mughals affected the countryside
solution: The chapter's overall message is that British colonial rule PROFOUNDLY TRANSFORMED the Indian countryside, in ways that created winners and losers and often deepened rural distress and provoked resistance. In Bengal, the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (under Cornwallis) fixed the revenue permanently and made zamindars the proprietors responsible for paying it under the harsh Sunset Law — leading, in the early decades, to widespread default and the auctioning of estates, various zamindari survival strategies (like fictitious sales), the ultimate burdening of the ryots, and the rise of powerful resident rich peasants (jotedars). In the Bombay Deccan, the ryotwari system imposed a high, revisable cash demand directly on the ryots, who, squeezed further by the collapse of the cotton boom after the American Civil War, fell deep into DEBT to moneylenders (sahukars) and lost land — culminating in the Deccan Riots of 1875, in which peasants attacked moneylenders and burnt their debt-bonds. And in the tribal tracts, peoples like the Santhals were settled (in the Damin-i-Koh) to clear forest and cultivate, but were exploited by dikus (moneylenders/traders) and the revenue burden, rising in the Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56 under Sidhu and Kanhu. Crucially, this whole history is reconstructed largely from COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS — revenue records, surveys, the Fifth Report (1813), and enquiry-commission reports (like the Deccan Riots Commission) — which are invaluable but reflect the OFFICIAL, colonial perspective and biases (often blaming moneylenders while excusing government policy, and obscuring peasants' own voices), and so must be read CRITICALLY. So the overall message is option 2.
